articles.title: VinFast VF MPV 7 Price Cut to Rs 20.39 Lakh (Nov 2026)
articles.categoryDescription: Recent news and new launches: vehicles, gadgets, AI and aviation, explained from official sources.
articles.excerpt: VinFast has cut the price of its VF MPV 7 electric seven-seater in India by Rs 4.1 lakh, from Rs 24.49 lakh to Rs 20.39 lakh ex-showroom, as reported on 4 November 2026.
blocks: VinFast has lowered the price of the VF MPV 7, its electric seven-seater in India, by Rs 4.1 lakh. The ex-showroom price moves from the launch price of Rs 24.49 lakh to Rs 20.39 lakh, according to reports dated 4 November 2026 from Autocar India and Rushlane. This article is accurate as of 4 November 2026.

**Old price:** Rs 24.49 lakh (ex-showroom), the price at launch on 15 April 2026.
**New price:** Rs 20.39 lakh (ex-showroom).
**Difference:** Rs 4.1 lakh.
**Variants:** both outlets describe one fully equipped version, so there is a single price to compare.
**Equipment and mechanicals:** Autocar India says they are unchanged.

Rushlane reports that the new price is also shown on VinFast's website. Neither report gives an exact date from which the new price applies, and neither quotes a VinFast statement about the reason for the change. Buyers who want to know whether the new price applies to a booking already made would need to ask VinFast or a dealer.
The car itself is described the same way in both reports. These figures are the ones the outlets report, and ARAI range is a test-cycle figure rather than a promise for daily driving.

**Battery:** 60.13 kWh.
**Claimed range:** 517 km on a full charge (ARAI-rated, per Autocar India).
**Motor:** one front-mounted motor, 204 PS (about 204 hp) and 280 Nm.
**Claimed 0 to 100 km/h:** under 9 seconds.
**Charging:** Autocar India lists 6.9 kW AC and 80 kW DC charging; Rushlane says VinFast claims 10% to 70% in about 30 minutes on a compatible DC charger.
**Size:** 4,740 mm long with a 2,840 mm wheelbase, three rows, up to seven seats.
**Boot:** 126 litres with all rows up, up to 1,240 litres with the rear rows folded (Rushlane).
How the price compares with other electric MPVs and SUVs
Both outlets place the VF MPV 7 against other electric family vehicles. Their price ranges are ex-showroom and are taken from the two reports; they are not identical, so treat them as indicative.

**Mahindra XEV 9S:** from about Rs 20.65 lakh (both outlets).
**Kia Carens Clavis EV:** Rs 18.04 lakh to Rs 25 lakh (Autocar India).
**MG Hector Tomahawk EV:** Autocar India lists Rs 20.25 lakh to Rs 24.25 lakh, while Rushlane lists a starting price of Rs 19.49 lakh. The two figures differ.
**BYD eMax 7:** from about Rs 27.9 lakh (both outlets).

At Rs 20.39 lakh, the VF MPV 7 is now priced a little below the Mahindra XEV 9S starting price quoted by both outlets, and above the starting prices quoted for the Carens Clavis EV and the Hector Tomahawk EV. Because the VinFast is sold in one configuration and the others in several, the starting price of a range and a single price are not like for like.

Rushlane reports that the VF MPV 7 sold 520 units between April and September 2026, about 3.91% of VinFast's 13,307 total India sales in that period, and suggests the launch price may have held sales back. Autocar India also describes the model's sales as having had a slow start. Neither outlet quotes VinFast on why the price was changed, so the link between the two is the outlets' reading, not a company statement.

Source note: this story is reported by two news outlets, and Rushlane says the new price appears on VinFast's website. We could not open a VinFast press release for the change. Check the price with VinFast or a dealer before relying on it.

The date from which the new price applies.
Whether bookings made at the old price are adjusted.
Whether any ownership schemes or incentives mentioned by Autocar India change the effective cost.

This is general information for readers following the Indian electric vehicle market, not a recommendation to buy. Prices in India vary by city because of taxes and registration, and ex-showroom prices exclude those costs.

sources.title: Vinfast VF MPV 7 price slashed by over Rs 4 lakh, Autocar India
VinFast VF MPV 7 price cut Rs 4.1 lakh, now costs Rs 20.39 lakh, Rushlane

articles.title: Nissan Magnite, Gravite Free CNG Kit Offer (Nov 2026)
articles.excerpt: Nissan India is offering a free government-approved CNG retrofit kit on select Magnite and Gravite variants until 16 November 2026, as reported on 4 November 2026.
blocks: Nissan Motor India is giving a government-approved CNG retrofit kit at no extra cost on selected variants of the Magnite and the Gravite, according to Autocar India and Rushlane on 4 November 2026. The offer runs until 16 November 2026. Without the offer, the kit is priced at Rs 74,999 for the Magnite and Rs 85,999 for the Gravite. This article is accurate as of 4 November 2026.

**What you get:** the CNG retrofit kit fitted free on eligible variants.
**Closing date:** 16 November 2026. Autocar India says the scheme runs until that date; Rushlane says bookings must be made before it.
**Kit warranty:** a third-party warranty of 3 years or 1,00,000 km, whichever comes first, on top of the standard vehicle warranty (both outlets).
**Local terms:** Autocar India quotes the fine print that benefits may vary by city and depend on stock.
Both outlets agree that only non-turbo versions qualify, because the CNG kit works with the 1.0-litre naturally aspirated petrol engine. They differ slightly on which entry variants are left out.

**Magnite:** all non-turbo variants except the base Visia manual and the Visia+ manual. Autocar India also excludes the Visia AMT; Rushlane lists the Visia EZ-Shift instead. These are the same automated manual version under two names, but we have not confirmed that, so check the exact variant with a dealer.
**Gravite:** the Tekna trim only.

Rushlane's opening lines swap the two kit prices, but later sections of the same article and Autocar India both give the figures below, which also match the article's closing numbers of about Rs 75,000 and Rs 86,000.

**Magnite kit:** normally Rs 74,999. Single cylinder in the boot (Rushlane).
**Gravite kit:** normally Rs 85,999. Two 25-litre cylinders, which Rushlane says keep the third row of seats usable.
**Engine:** 1.0-litre naturally aspirated petrol, with a 5-speed manual or 5-speed AMT. Autocar India gives about 63 hp and 72 Nm on CNG.
**Claimed CNG mileage:** 19.3 km/kg for the Gravite (Autocar India). Nissan had not disclosed a figure for the Magnite in that report.

**Gravite Tekna:** Rs 8.08 lakh to Rs 9.09 lakh (Autocar India).
**Magnite non-turbo, Acenta manual and above:** Rs 6.87 lakh to Rs 9.31 lakh (Autocar India).

A retrofit kit is fitted to a petrol car after it is built, which is different from a factory-fitted CNG model. Nissan describes its kits as government-approved. The petrol tank stays, so the car can run on either fuel.

Autocar India reports that buyers who do not take the kit can choose other benefits instead: up to Rs 1 lakh plus a gold coin on the Magnite, and up to Rs 55,000 plus a gold coin on the Gravite. Rushlane says Nissan has announced no other festive benefits for these models. The two reports therefore differ on this point.

Source note: this story rests on two news outlets. Nissan India's own news page, when we opened it on 4 November 2026, did not list the offer, and it points to a monthly offers section for current schemes. Confirm variants, kit price and the closing date with a Nissan dealer.

The exact variant names excluded from the Magnite offer.
City-by-city availability.
Whether Nissan will extend the offer after 16 November.
This is general information about a manufacturer's promotion, not buying advice. Fuel prices, running costs and boot space change with the kit, so compare using Nissan's own figures.

articles.title: How Automatic Gearboxes Work: Torque Converter and Gears
articles.excerpt: A conventional automatic gearbox joins the engine to planetary gears through a fluid-filled torque converter and picks ratios with hydraulic clutches. Here is how each part works.
blocks: A conventional automatic gearbox changes gear without a clutch pedal by using three ideas together: a fluid-filled torque converter in place of a clutch, planetary gear sets that make the different ratios, and hydraulic pressure that decides which gears are engaged. This article explains each part in plain terms. Other automatic designs, such as CVTs and dual-clutch gearboxes, work differently and are covered briefly at the end.
Why a car needs a gearbox at all

A petrol or diesel engine works well only inside a band of speeds. A gearbox lets the wheels turn at a very different speed from the engine: a low gear gives strong pulling force for starting, and a high gear lets the engine turn slowly at cruising speed. A manual gearbox needs a clutch pedal to disconnect the engine while the driver swaps gears. A conventional automatic does both jobs on its own.
The torque converter: a clutch made of fluid
Between the engine and the gearbox sits a torque converter, a doughnut-shaped housing filled with transmission fluid. It has three main parts, described on Wikipedia's torque converter page.

**Impeller:** the input side, spun by the engine. Its vanes throw fluid outward.
**Turbine:** the output side, connected to the gearbox. The moving fluid pushes it round.
**Stator:** a small wheel between the two. It redirects fluid coming back from the turbine so that it helps the impeller instead of fighting it. It sits on a one-way clutch, so it can turn forward but not backward.

A simpler fluid coupling has only the first two parts and cannot increase torque. The stator is what allows a converter to multiply torque when the car moves off. According to Wikipedia, typical car converters multiply torque by about 1.8 to 2.5 times at stall, which is the moment when the engine is working but the turbine is held still. As the car speeds up, the multiplication falls. When the turbine reaches roughly 90% of the impeller speed, the unit acts like a plain fluid coupling.
Because the link is fluid, the engine keeps running when the car is stopped in gear. This is why an automatic can idle at a red light with the brake pressed and does not stall.

Fluid always slips a little, which wastes fuel. Many converters therefore contain a lock-up clutch that joins impeller and turbine mechanically at cruising speed. Wikipedia says such clutches became nearly universal in cars after returning in the late 1970s for fuel economy.
Planetary gear sets: many ratios in a small space

Instead of pairs of gears on parallel shafts, most automatics use planetary gear sets. One set has four kinds of part, according to Wikipedia's planetary gear page: a central sun gear, two to four planet gears that mesh with it, a carrier that holds the planets, and an outer ring gear with teeth on the inside.

The trick is to hold one part still while another is driven. With the ring gear held and the sun gear as input, the carrier turns more slowly than the sun, giving a reduction. Hold a different part and the same set gives a different ratio, or reverses direction. Several sets can be placed one after another in a single housing. The same page names compound designs used in automatics, including the Simpson set with three forward gears and the Lepelletier set with six.
Clutches and bands choose the gear

What holds a part still? Band brakes that clamp a drum, and multi-plate clutches made of friction discs that alternate with steel plates. Hydraulic pistons squeeze them together or let them go. YourMechanic's explainer says the discs grip the steel plates gradually, which is why a gear change feels smooth. One-way sprag clutches also carry torque in normal shifts and release by themselves when the next gear takes over, as noted by Wikipedia, so the timing of the other clutches is less critical.

A pump, driven by the converter housing and so turning at engine speed, draws fluid from the sump and pressurises it. A valve body sends that pressure to the right clutches and bands. Older gearboxes used a governor linked to the output shaft, which let in more fluid as the car went faster, and a vacuum modulator that sensed engine load. Newer ones use solenoids controlled by a transmission or engine control computer, which reads speed sensors and the throttle position.
Since the pump runs off the engine, there is no pressure when the engine is off. Wikipedia gives this as the reason most automatic cars cannot be push-started.

**1940 model year:** General Motors' Hydra-Matic, using a fluid coupling and three planetary sets for four forward speeds, became the first mass-produced automatic.
**1948:** Buick's Dynaflow was the first automatic with a torque converter.
**1964:** GM's Turbo Hydramatic used a converter and helped fix the P-R-N-D-L selector layout.
**1989:** Nissan's Jatco 5R01 was the first electronically controlled five-speed.
**2002 and 2007:** ZF's six-speed in the BMW 7 Series and Toyota's AA80E mark the first six- and eight-speed units, with a ten-speed in the 2017 Lexus LC.
These dates come from Wikipedia's automatic transmission page, which itself notes that the claim for an earlier 1904 gearbox is unverified.

**CVT:** a continuously variable transmission with no fixed gears, usually two pulleys joined by a belt or chain.
**Dual-clutch (DCT):** two clutches, one for odd gears and one for even, so the next gear is ready before the change.
**Automated manual (AMT):** a manual gearbox where the clutch and shifting are done by actuators.
Wikipedia says conventional automatics are about 86% to 94% efficient, and that real-world tests in 2022 found manuals 2% to 5% more fuel efficient in typical driving. Results vary by car and driver.
YourMechanic notes that transmission fluid lubricates and cools the parts, so low or burnt fluid is a common warning sign. For any actual fault or service interval, follow the car's own manual.

sources.title: How an Automatic Transmission Works, YourMechanic

articles.title: Countersteering: How Motorcycles and Bikes Turn
articles.excerpt: To turn right on a bike or motorcycle, a rider first nudges the bars left. Here is why that starts the lean, what keeps two-wheelers upright and where the science is still debated.
blocks: To turn right on a bicycle or motorcycle, a rider first pushes the right handlebar forward, which briefly points the front wheel left. That small push makes the bike lean right, and the lean is what carries it round the corner. The technique is called countersteering. It works on any single-track vehicle, and most riders do it without noticing.

Wikipedia describes the sequence like this. To go right, the rider applies a brief torque to the bars towards the left. The front wheel turns left, and the tyre contact patches move out from under the bike, so the bike leans to the right. The rider, or the bike's own stability, then steers the wheel back to the right and the turn begins. Steering is then held to keep the lean.

The first input can be very short. Wikipedia says it may last as little as 0.125 seconds, so many riders are unaware that they do it. At low speed it is small and mixed with balance corrections. At higher speed the bike resists more, so a given push on the bars changes the lean by less, and the rider must push harder or longer.

A moving bike that turns without leaning would tip outward, like a person carrying a heavy bag round a bend. To stay balanced the rider and bike must lean inward. The lean angle follows a simple formula given on Wikipedia: the angle equals the arctangent of speed squared divided by gravity times turn radius. Its worked example is a 10 m radius turn at 10 m/s, which needs about 45.6 degrees of lean. Faster speed or a tighter turn needs more lean.

A University of Guelph science-communication article, written by an undergraduate student, explains the start of the lean in terms of forces. Steering one way sends the wheels sideways under the rider. Because the bike is now tilted, the ground pushes back along the direction of the lean, and the lean increases. This is a simplified account, but it matches the same sequence.
Why a bike stays upright at all

Balance comes from a mixture of effects. Wikipedia's bicycle and motorcycle dynamics page lists geometry, how mass is spread, gyroscopic effects and forward speed, and says that claims that any one of them is solely responsible have been discredited.

**Trail:** the front wheel touches the ground slightly behind the point where the steering axis meets the road. When the bike leans, the ground force steers the front wheel into the lean, which helps to catch a fall.
**Gyroscopic effect:** a spinning front wheel resists being tilted and turns towards the lean. It adds a quick roll moment when the rider applies steering. Wikipedia's countersteering page gives an example of about 12% of the roll moment from tyre forces for a motorcycle at 22 m/s.
**Speed:** between a low and a high speed range, some bikes can steer themselves upright even with no rider. Higher speed makes small steering changes more effective, so balance is easier.

The Guelph article calls trail the single largest contributor to a bicycle's stability, citing a 1982 paper in the American Journal of Physics. The Wikipedia page describes later research in which David Jones (1970) showed gyroscopic effects are not necessary for balance, and Kooijman and colleagues (2011, in Science) built a bicycle with negative trail and counter-rotating wheels that was still self-stable. Their conclusion, as summarised by Wikipedia, is that neither effect is sufficient by itself or strictly necessary, though both can help hands-free stability. We could not open the Science paper itself, so this relies on the Wikipedia summary.

Wikipedia reports that the Motorcycle Safety Foundation teaches countersteering in all its courses and that it appears in the rider manuals and tests of several US states. It cites the Hurt Report, an older study of motorcycle crashes, which found that many riders braked too hard, skidded the rear wheel and could not swerve. Countersteering is described as the quickest way to change direction in an emergency. Slogans such as press left to lean left, go left are used in training.
Shifting body weight alone can start a lean on a light bicycle, but Wikipedia says it is much less effective on a heavy motorcycle. Three-wheelers that cannot lean do not countersteer.
This is general information, not riding instruction. Anyone learning to ride should do so through an approved course with a qualified instructor.

sources.title: Turning right to go left, University of Guelph, Department of Physics
